title: Seven ears of grain
hook: a gift in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears, a hundred grains each (2:261)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a hundred years asleep, 'Uzayr's, and your line, he can revive what is dead. What did you give one more look? Today, life again, this time out of a single seed. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

Pull one stalk of wheat from a field and look at the top. The head, the ear, is packed with grains in neat rows. Any farmer knows the trade: you put one grain in the ground, and months later you hold dozens. It's arithmetic and hope in the same handful. Right after three stories about God bringing the dead to life, al-Baqarah turns to the field and does some arithmetic of its own. Today: seven ears of grain.
screen: `ONE STALK OF WHEAT.` → `ONE GRAIN IN, DOZENS OUT.` → `AL-BAQARAH DOES THE ARITHMETIC.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred sixty-one, in Pickthall's words: “The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.” Do the math. One grain, seven ears, a hundred each: seven hundred. And the verse doesn't stop there. It adds: God multiplies for whom He wills. Seven hundred isn't the ceiling. The placement matters. The surah has just shown a dead town, a donkey's bones, four birds, all brought to life. Now a seed, buried and dead-looking, brings up a field. Giving is presented the same way: something you let go of into the ground, which looks lost, and comes back multiplied. Two hadith fill in the picture. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim says a good deed is written as ten, up to seven hundred times, and many times more. And another hadith in Bukhari says that whoever gives even the value of a single date from honest earnings, God accepts it with His right hand and raises it the way one of you raises a young horse, until it becomes like a mountain. Notice the size of the gift in that hadith: one date. The grain in the verse is tiny too. Nothing in this passage asks for a large gift. It asks for a real one, given for God's sake, from what's honestly yours, and then let go. In the verse, the arithmetic is God's. One grain, seven hundred.
screen: `ONE GRAIN, SEVEN EARS, A HUNDRED EACH` · `NOT THE CEILING` · `BURIED, LOST-LOOKING, MULTIPLIED` · `ONE DATE BECOMES A MOUNTAIN`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give a small amount today. Not a big decision. A coin, a dollar, a meal, ten minutes of help. Sit now, and choose where it goes: a charity, a neighbor, someone on the street, a colleague who's struggling. Picture handing it over and then letting it go, like a grain into the soil, without needing to see what grows. Hold that picture while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Seven ears of grain. Al-Baqarah's picture of giving: one grain that grows seven ears, a hundred grains each, and God multiplies further for whom He wills. Today's word.
Your line: one grain, seven hundred. Today, give the small thing you chose, and don't count what comes of it. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in amounts large and small, often citing 2:261 and the hadith that even a date given from honest earnings grows like a mountain.

original.note: Arabic: ears of grain (singular sunbulah); the seven ears of 2:261.

trapdoor: what you thought: a promise that charity pays back.
what it means: giving pictured as a seed: let go into the ground, lost-looking, and multiplied by God.
what a scholar hears: the verse's place after the three resurrection stories of 2:258–260, and the hadith qudsi's scale of ten to seven hundred and beyond.
